The same next-token principle

pθ(xₜ | x₁, …, xₜ₋₁) = [softmax(zₜ)]ₓₜ

The context produces logits z, which softmax converts into a distribution over the vocabulary. The selected token extends the context for the next step.

Chosen token probability—
Token surprise · nats—
surprise = −ln p(chosen token)

Surprise describes this generated token. It is not a training loss curve: there is no backpropagation or weight update here.

How to explain this in the seminar +

Connect it to GPT-1

Both demonstrations use the autoregressive idea: predict the next token from the preceding context. During language-model training, the observed next token supplies the target and its negative log probability supplies a learning signal.

This page runs modern Qwen. Its tokenizer, architecture and instruction behavior differ from GPT-1. Instruction examples demonstrate prompting, not the supervised fine-tuning procedure in the GPT-1 paper.

What is actually measured?

Token IDs, generated tokens and log probabilities come from the running server. Automatic mode buffers real model output and reveals it at your chosen presentation speed, with the matching probability chart at every step. This speed is not a model throughput measurement. Pause keeps unrevealed tokens for Resume. Generation stops at the model's end token or the demo's 2048-token context limit.

Manual batches appear after their request completes. Selecting a token shows the distribution from that generation step. The server does not expose attention maps, gradients or training checkpoints here. For optimization and convergence, open the real tiny-model training lesson.
